newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks rebound from last week's plunge.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks rebound from last week's plunge.

text.p: Asian stocks bounced back on Monday from last week's strong correction sparked by fears the U.S. central bank was about to clamp down on ebullient markets.
Japan's Nikkei 225 surged 327.01 points, or 1.61 percent, to close at 20,603.71, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index put on 41.50 points to end at 13,144.23, or 0.32 percent higher.
Australian stocks also closed higher while bourses in Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia were trading in positive territory.

Steep declines on Friday were blamed on investors' reaction to comments by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan. But they were buying again on Monday because of a better U.S. inflation outlook and the opportunity to pick up bargains, traders said.
"The market did a kneejerk reaction to what Alan Greenspan said (on Friday). But today, the market looks pretty good," said an institutional salesman at a Malaysian brokerage.
On Friday, Asian markets led a worldwide slide in stock prices as the first to react to Greenspan's remarks in a speech on Thursday night.
The Fed chief spoke of "irrational exuberance" infecting markets and said the direction of inflation was impossible to determine.

Asian markets took his remarks as a signal that the U.S. central bank would raise interest rates. Losses on the Nikkei were the sharpest since April 1995, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng index suffered its biggest one-day fall in about nine months.
But the reaction in the United States was more moderate. The Dow Jones index of 30 industrials clawed back from a 140-point drop to finish down 55 points on Friday.
"It was only natural that the Nikkei average rebounded since the U.S. markets' losses were not that big," Harushige Kobayashi, Yamaichi Securities deputy general manager, said on Monday.
Kuala Lumpur stayed positive in the afternoon with buyers picking up stocks cheapened by Friday's fall, traders said. The key Composite Index was up 8.79 points, or 0.74 percent, to 1,200.11.
In Singapore the Straits Times Industrials Index was up 8.09 points at 2,198.48. Dealers said the market was underpinned by a reassuring figures on U.S. inflation.
U.S. unemployment data for November, released on Friday, were weaker than expected, opening the way for a recovery by U.S. Treasuries.
"This helped to reassure the market that a (U.S.) rate hike is quite unlikely," one Singapore dealer said.

Australian shares bounced to a firmer close, ending 25.9 points, or 1.12 percent higher, at 2,339.8. Seoul shares, however, gave up early gains to end at a new three-year low on fears of labour strife and share oversupply, traders said. The composite index fell 3.94 points or 0.57 percent to a provisional close of 692.17.
Thai stocks slipped in thin trade ahead of a holiday on Tuesday. The SET index was at 876.04, down 0.85 points.
